Hey @pcbeingused333, thank you for your contribution!

The gap is real and the change matches the asyncio pool, including the race fix in the second commit. One change is needed before merge: `close()` should not just drop the pending MOVING cleanup. A sync pool can be reused after `close()`, and today the timer still reverts the temporary host and relaxed timeouts after the TTL. With this patch they stay in `connection_kwargs` permanently, so every connection created after reuse inherits the MOVING state.

Please run the pending cleanups on close (call `handle_node_moved_notification` for each pending handoff) instead of only cancelling them, and apply the same change to `AsyncMaintNotificationsPoolHandler.cancel_scheduled_tasks()`, since asyncio has the same gap. Your offer in the thread covers exactly this. A test that closes a pool mid-MOVING, reuses it, and asserts the kwargs are reverted on both stacks would cover it.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Serialize timer cancellation with callback completion**

When another notification holds `_lock` as a timer expires and another thread calls `close()`, `run()` has already discarded the timer before its callback can obtain that lock. The snapshot here therefore sees no timer, so `close()` can return and then `run_proactive_reconnect` or cleanup can mutate a closed (or already reused) pool; concurrent mutation can also make these unlocked set snapshots raise. Keep timers registered through callback completion and coordinate/wait for cancellation, as the async mirror does.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Wait for the timer callback deterministically**

On a loaded CI worker, a `threading.Timer(0.2, ...)` is not guaranteed to be scheduled by the time this 0.4-second sleep returns, so the following `assert_called_once_with` can fail even when `disconnect()` correctly leaves the timer active. Have the callback signal a `threading.Event` (with a generous timeout), or drive a fake timer, instead of depending on wall-clock scheduling.

### Timer cancellation is not thread-safe **Medium Severity** `cancel_scheduled_tasks` mutates `_scheduled_timers` and `_pending_handoffs` without `_lock`, while each timer removes itself from the set before the callback and is never joined. Closing the pool can race with a firing or newly scheduled MOVING timer, so `close()` may raise, leave a non-daemon timer running, or emit `MaintenanceCompletedEvent` twice.
Additional Locations (1) - [`redis/maint_notifications.py#L1064-L1098`](https://github.com/redis/redis-py/blob/4a704ab1522229162168df400b874c915f23bd1b/redis/maint_notifications.py#L1064-L1098)

Fixed in ed8db7ff: each timer stays registered until its callback finishes, the callback runs under the handler lock and is skipped once cancelled, and `cancel_scheduled_tasks()` snapshots and clears the timers and pending handoffs under the same lock; added a test for a timer firing while `close()` cancels.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Restore MOVING settings before dropping cleanup timers**

When an application uses this `ConnectionPool` again after `close()` (which remains possible because `close()` only disconnects and no closed flag is checked), clearing these timers drops the only call to `handle_node_moved_notification`; consequently `connection_kwargs` remains `MOVING` with the replacement host and relaxed timeouts indefinitely, so later connections can target the stale endpoint and subsequent maintenance events are handled under stale state. Revert the active handoff before discarding its cleanup, and make the same lifecycle correction in the async mirror.

This mirrors the asyncio pool, whose `cancel_scheduled_tasks()` already cancels the MOVING cleanups on close without reverting them. Running the pending cleanups on close (reverting the kwargs and connection settings) would be a lifecycle change for both stacks; I can add it to both here if that's the behaviour you want for a pool reused after `close()`.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject notification handlers invalidated by close**

When an in-use connection begins processing a MOVING push after `_on_close()` has taken its timer snapshot but while `disconnect()` is running, its handler can add a new cleanup timer after cancellation (`redis/connection.py:4302-4304` explicitly allows disconnecting connections used by other threads). `close()` then returns with a non-daemon timer that can later mutate a closed or already reused pool. Unlike the earlier expiry-callback race, this timer is created after the cancellation snapshot, so retaining existing timers through callback completion does not cover it; invalidate pre-close connection handlers or make scheduling atomic with the whole close transition in both stacks.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Clear dedupe state for handoffs ended by close**

When a pool is closed and reused before the handoff TTL expires, the server sends the still-active MOVING notification to the replacement connection during setup (the scenario at `tests/test_scenario/test_maint_notifications.py:1223-1251` relies on this). Rejecting those would need a closed state on the handler that is cleared when the pool is used again, since the pool can be reused after `close()` and a redelivered MOVING then has to be applied. **<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reset the inherited handler lock before close**

When a process forks while another parent thread holds the maintenance handler's `RLock` (for example while processing MOVING), the child can call `ConnectionPool.close()` and block forever at this new hook: `_checkpid()` is not reached until `disconnect()` on the following line, and unlike `_fork_lock` this inherited handler lock has no timeout or child reset. I reproduced this with a RESP3 pool by holding `handler._lock` in a thread, forking, and calling `close()` in the child; it only exited via an alarm. Reset or bypass the inherited handler state before acquiring it in `close()`.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Process pending handoffs when no tasks remain**

If `aclose()` is cancelled after it cancels the timer tasks but while an immediate MOVING cleanup is waiting for the pool lock, the tasks' done callbacks empty `_scheduled_tasks` while `_pending_handoffs` remains populated. Retrying `aclose()` then returns here, skips cleanup, and leaves `connection_kwargs` on the temporary host and relaxed timeouts even though disconnect completes; this is reproducible by holding `pool._lock`, starting and cancelling `aclose()`, then releasing the lock and retrying. This one is broader than the close path: the handler lock is shared by every connection's handler and isn't reset in a forked child, so any MOVING handling in the child could hit it, not only `close()`. Thanks, this was a real regression. Closing the pool now runs the pending cleanups, and `handle_node_moved_notification` only reports `MaintenanceCompletedEvent` when it reverted the kwargs, so a handoff superseded by a newer MOVING lost the completed event that pairs its started event (the asyncio `cancel_scheduled_tasks()` used to dispatch it for every pending handoff). The handler now returns whether it reverted the kwargs, and `close()` / `aclose()` dispatch the completed event for the handoffs where it did not, on both stacks. New tests close a pool with two overlapping MOVING notifications and expect a completed event for each one; they fail on the previous commit and pass with 9780a8a5.

If `close()` cleanup raises after one matching connection has been reset—for example, a concurrent disconnect closes the socket between `update_current_socket_timeout()` obtaining it and resetting its timeout—this early discard removes the handoff before later connections are reset. `cancel_scheduled_tasks()` has already cleared every timer, so a retry sees neither timers nor pending handoffs; those later disconnected connections retain their MOVING host/timeouts and use them when the pool is reused. Retain the handoff until the reset succeeds, as the async implementation does.

### Reentrant close duplicates completed events **Medium Severity** `cancel_scheduled_tasks()` walks a snapshot of `_pending_handoffs` and, when cleanup does not revert kwargs, always emits `MaintenanceCompletedEvent`. A completion listener that calls `close()` reenters this method (the handler uses a reentrant `RLock`) and already finishes the remaining handoffs. The outer loop then calls `handle_node_moved_notification()` again for those same notifications, gets `False`, and dispatches a second completed event. The asyncio path skips handoffs that are no longer pending; the sync loop does not. Listeners that pair start/complete events then over-count completion when a pool is closed mid-overlapping MOVING.
Additional Locations (1) - [`redis/asyncio/maint_notifications.py#L332-L342`](https://github.com/redis/redis-py/blob/ced9fc32f2ac140463da267244bc43d5c75af213/redis/asyncio/maint_notifications.py#L332-L342)

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Retain each handoff's config during close cleanup**

When `update_maint_notifications_config()` replaces the config while a MOVING handoff is pending—for example, it turns `proactive_reconnect` off or sets `relaxed_timeout=-1`—this close path executes the cleanup through the pool's root handler, so `handle_node_moved_notification()` reads the new flags instead of those that originally set the per-connection temporary values. The cleanup then marks matching connections `NONE` without restoring their replacement host or relaxed timeout; `close()` disconnects them, and a later pool reuse reconnects those retained objects with stale settings because the canceled original timer can no longer correct them. Retain the cleanup policy/config per handoff here and in `AsyncMaintNotificationsPoolHandler.cancel_scheduled_tasks()`.

Thanks, both were real. `close()` discarded the handoff before running its cleanup, so a cleanup that raised halfway (a connection disconnected under it makes `settimeout` raise `EBADF`) could not be retried: the timers were already cancelled and a second `close()` found nothing pending. The handoff is now discarded after the cleanup, as the asyncio handler does. And two concurrent `aclose()` calls could both run the cleanup of the same handoff, the second one taking the already-reverted kwargs for a superseded handoff and reporting a second `MaintenanceCompletedEvent`; each closer now re-checks the handoff under the handler lock and runs the cleanup there. Two new tests cover a `close()` retried after a failing cleanup and `asyncio.gather(pool.aclose(), pool.aclose())` over one pending handoff; both fail on the previous commit.

Thanks, both were regressions of this PR. The discard now happens once the state reset is done and before the completion listeners run, on both stacks, so a listener that closes the pool no longer re-runs the cleanup and reports a second completion. And `close()` / `aclose()` now disconnect in a `finally` block, so a MOVING cleanup that raises still closes every connection; the exception propagates and the handoff stays pending for a retried close. Three new tests cover the listener that closes the pool and a failing cleanup on each stack; they fail on the previous commit.
